title: 'Artificial' movie poster mimics AI slop, but was hand-drawn
excerpt: Neon's Artificial poster hides a sinking bridge, an upside-down plane, and other details designed to look like AI errors.
content_html:
A new poster for OpenAI movie 'Artificial' calls out AI slop in the most human way possible

By Georgia Hennessy

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-20T13:10:50.736Z

A new poster for "Artificial" — Luca Guadagnino's movie about OpenAI — is full of the kind of mistakes you might expect from an AI image generator.

There's one key difference, however: A human artist put them there.

At first glance, it looks like a pretty normal poster: Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, stands on a wooded path overlooking San Francisco Bay.

Look longer, and you start to notice strange, uncanny details.

A face resembling Pinocchio peers out of a tree trunk. The branches morph into snakes at the tips. The Golden Gate Bridge appears to sink beneath the water, and a plane flies upside down overhead. The backpack's logo looks like garbled AI text. Even Andrew Garfield's face looks a little unfamiliar.

Neon, the film's distributor, credited the poster to artist Mike Thompson and creative agency Gravillis Inc. A small note on the image reads "Artwork made by Humans."

The company also shared a video showing the artwork's creation, using dialogue from the film as the image takes shape.

Garfield's Altman describes an uncertain future and says, "We get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world."

He ends with: "I'm so excited to see it."

Artificial follows the rise of OpenAI and a struggle over who controls increasingly powerful AI technology, with Yura Borisov and Monica Barbaro in supporting roles.

The story also revisits the 2023 leadership crisis at OpenAI, when the company's board fired Altman as CEO and reinstated him days later after a backlash from employees and investors.

The day before the poster was released, Altman was asked about the film at a New York Times DealBook summit. Altman said a movie about him would have seemed strange 20 years ago.

Now, he said, it does not rank among "the top 10 weirdest things about my life." He pointed instead to the responsibility of developing AI amid concerns about its effects.
